title: Al-Matin, the Firm
hookLine: the Firm, whose strength never wavers
tomorrow: guardian, or friend? one Name, two English words.

lines: FULL AT BREAKFAST, RED BY DINNER.
WHY IS THE FIRM NEXT TO FOOD?
cards: A phone at full charge at breakfast is blinking red by dinner. Sprinters fade in the last stretch. Plenty of good intentions are gone by Thursday.
Everything we have runs on a curve. Now, a strange spot in the Qur'an. In Surah adh-Dhariyat, the Name Al-Matin turns up, and it isn't in a battle or a storm.
It sits right next to food. Why would the Firm be standing beside livelihood?

teach.b: Here's the verse in Pickthall's words: "Lo! Allah! He it is that giveth livelihood, the Lord of unbreakable might." Pickthall doesn't write "the firm". He writes unbreakable might.
And just before it, Allah says He wants no provision from people and doesn't ask to be fed. So here's the puzzle solved. The strength in this verse isn't a burst, like lifting a car off someone.

It's the kind that never dips: the provision that arrives again tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after that, from One who runs on nothing. That's Al-Matin. Firm, the way the ground under a house is firm.
You only notice it by the fact that it's still there. No person gets unbreakable might. But there's a human-sized version, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, named it.
He said the deeds most loved by Allah are the most consistent ones, even if they're small.

teach.h: SMALL AND STEADY, STILL THERE THURSDAY.
teach.b: Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: small and steady beating big and rare isn't a productivity tip somebody invented last year. It's a hadith. Two minutes of reading every day outlasts a four-hour Saturday.
One kind word daily outlasts one grand apology.
Firm isn't loud. Firm is still there on Thursday.

how: Muslims often keep small daily practices, a page of Qur'an, set dhikr after prayer, steadily rather than in bursts, following the hadith that the most loved deeds are the most consistent.

o: the Strict, who never bends a rule
the Firm, whose strength never wavers
the Heavy, who weighs every deed

games.q: what keeps going — tap the pairs.
p: the Name's neighbor in the verse
the most consistent, even if small

s: the hadith says the deeds Allah loves most are the biggest ones
the most consistent, even if small.
"the Lord of unbreakable might," right after "giveth livelihood."
in this verse firm is steady: strength that keeps arriving, not strength that hits hard.

games.q: your cousin wants to read more Qur'an. week one she read for four hours on saturday and nothing since. she asks what to do. what fits Al-Matin?
o: save it for weekends, when there's real time.
a little every day, even on the busy ones.
wait until she can commit to hours at a time.
games.why: the deeds most loved by Allah are the most consistent, even if small. firm isn't the big session; it's the one still happening on Thursday.

practice: Choose one tiny thing you could do at the same time every day this week: a page of reading, a glass of water at dawn, one message to a grandparent. Make it small enough that a bad day can't break it.
Then sit for two minutes with both feet flat on the floor, and with each breath let the plan settle: same time, same small thing.

wordCard.voice: Al-Matin. The Firm: unbreakable might, the strength that hasn't faded by the end of the day.

orig.note: Arabic: the Firm. in 51:58 Pickthall gives it as 'unbreakable might'.

carryVoice: One word for the road: firm, like a habit too small for a bad day to break. Day fifteen twenty-eight, done.
